definition.text: How efficiently energy passes from one trophic level to the next.

facts.text: Transfer between levels is generally inefficient: each level's net production is usually only about 10% of the level below.
Energy is lost through non-predatory death, egestion and respiration; halving at each of these three steps leaves about one-eighth, roughly ten percent.
It combines exploitation, assimilation and net production efficiencies, equal to consumer production divided by prey production.
Edible calories returned per calorie of cultivation energy are 18.1% for chicken, 6.7% for grass-fed beef and 0.9% for shrimp, versus 123% for potatoes, 250% for corn and 415% for soy.
So it is more energy-efficient to eat from lower trophic levels.
In 1999, 10.5% of the 28,400 terawatt-hours of energy used in the US went into food production.

definition.text: The rule of thumb that only about ten percent of food energy passing from one trophic level to the next is stored as new flesh.

facts.text: The rest is lost in transfer, used in respiration or lost through incomplete digestion.
It is credited to Raymond Lindeman (1942), though he did not call it a law and cited efficiencies from 0.1% to 37.5%.
In the standard example, of 10,000 J of sunlight plants take 100 J, a deer 10 J, a wolf 1 J, and a human eating the wolf 0.1 J.

title: Marine ecological efficiency
article: Ecological efficiency#Ecological efficiency in the marine environment

definition.text: The generally higher efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels in the sea than on land.

facts.text: Transfer from phytoplankton to herbivorous zooplankton is estimated at about 20%, compared with 10% on land.
Phytoplankton biomass can turn over 100–300 times a year, while land plants turn over only 0.5 to 2.0 times.
Coastal upwelling zones may have as few as three trophic levels and support whales, while open oceans can have six and support only small tuna and squid at the top.

definition.text: A diagram showing the biomass or productivity at each trophic level of an ecosystem, with producers at the base.

facts.text: A pyramid of energy shows energy kept as new biomass at each level, a pyramid of biomass shows the living matter present, and a pyramid of numbers counts individuals.
Energy pyramids are normally upright, but biomass pyramids can be inverted in the sea and number pyramids when many beetles feed on one tree.
In a pond, the phytoplankton present at any moment weigh less than the fish and insects, because they reproduce fast but live briefly.
Only 1 to 2 percent of the Sun's energy is absorbed by photosynthesis and turned into food.
Charles Elton developed the pyramid of numbers in 1927; Bodenheimer expressed it in biomass in 1938, and the energy pyramid draws on Hutchinson and Lindeman (1942).

definition.text: The study of how the balance of energy and chemical elements shapes living things and their interactions in ecosystems.

facts.text: It focuses on mismatches between what organisms need and what their food contains: termites have a carbon:nitrogen ratio of about 5 yet eat wood with a ratio of 300–1000.
Plants and algae vary widely in their elemental make-up, whereas animals keep a nearly fixed composition, a trait called stoichiometric homeostasis.
Lake algae and detritus range in C:P ratio from 100 to 1000, while the zooplankton Daphnia stays near 80:1.
Nitrogen and phosphorus pollution from farming can boost stream producers and ripple up the food web.
